title: POWER4 system microarchitecture
decision: Committed from the outset to delivering best-of-breed operating frequencies; revamped chip design with new transistor-level tools and transformed complex control logic into regular dataflow constructs.
alternatives_or_rejected: Implicitly rejected a lower-frequency, more complex-control-logic design style; the paper states complex control logic was transformed into regular dataflow constructs to hit frequency goals.
rationale: To maintain a leadership position in processor frequency; additionally the system was designed so that system balance is preserved as technology improvements raise processor frequency over time.
outcome: The POWER4 chip shipped at >1.3 GHz (per companion circuit-design paper); the paper reports POWER4 systems were offered at more than one frequency and bus frequencies scale with processor frequency to maintain system balance.

title: POWER4 system microarchitecture
where_in_paper: POWER4 chip — dual processors / Core Interface Unit
decision: Put two processor cores on a single POWER4 chip sharing a unified on-chip L2 (three autonomous L2 controllers) via a crossbar Core Interface Unit (CIU).
alternatives_or_rejected: Rejected building a single monolithic high-ILP uniprocessor; the paper's guiding principle favors SMP optimization, using 'a large number of transistors to improve total system performance' in an SMP-optimized design rather than maximizing a single core.
rationale: Servers process disparate information with multiple concurrent processes; SMP optimization lets a large number of transistors improve total system performance. The CIU crossbar feeds 32 bytes/cycle from each of the three L2 controllers to either core's I- or D-cache, enabling efficient on-chip data sharing.
outcome: The POWER4 chip integrates two processor cores, an on-chip unified L2, and the CIU crossbar on a single die (174M transistors per the companion circuit paper) as the basic building block for SMP systems.

title: POWER4 system microarchitecture
decision: Designed the entire system together up front — processor, memory subsystem, I/O bridge chips, process technology, and packaging — as a single synergistic design rather than optimizing the processor core alone.
alternatives_or_rejected: Rejected a processor-centric design isolated from the rest of the system; the paper argues 'we designed the entire system together, from the processor to memory and I/O bridge chips' because 'a new high-performance processor needs a new subsystem to feed it effectively.'
rationale: To optimize the system, the full design was conceived up front so that the marriage of process technology, packaging, and microarchitecture allowed software to exploit them, and the processor core was made to 'fit effectively in this environment.'
outcome: POWER4 is described not merely as a chip but as 'an architecture within which a set of chips are designed together to realize a system,' forming SMPs up to 32-way.

title: POWER4 system microarchitecture
decision: Used a distributed-switch interconnect fabric and a multi-chip-module hierarchy: four POWER4 chips per module form an 8-way SMP; four modules interconnect to form a 32-way SMP.
alternatives_or_rejected: The paper presents the distributed-switch topology as 'new to the industry,' implicitly contrasting with prior centralized / bus-based SMP interconnect approaches, though the paper does not detail specific alternative topologies it evaluated.
rationale: Needed to interconnect POWER4 chips to form symmetric multiprocessors of any size up to a 32-way SMP; each chip carries five primary interfaces (logical 16-byte on-module buses, 8-byte off-module buses, 16-byte L3 buses, GX I/O buses, JTAG) that scale with processor frequency to preserve system balance.
outcome: POWER4 systems scale from 8-way (one MCM) to 32-way (four interconnected MCMs) SMPs; all buses except JTAG scale with processor frequency.

title: POWER4 system microarchitecture
decision: Adopted a pervasive RAS philosophy that eliminates outages and provides redundancy where errors can't be eliminated; where possible, transforms hard machine stops (checkstops) into synchronous machine interrupts to software so the system can circumvent problems.
alternatives_or_rejected: Explicitly rejected the older approach of 'achieving high levels of reliability only by choosing reliable parts and incorporating ECC logic into major arrays'; instead required an approach that eliminates outages and adds redundancy.
rationale: Servers had evolved toward continuous operation; mainframe-class RAS attributes were brought into POWER4 systems, requiring elimination of outages and transformation of hard stops into recoverable software interrupts wherever possible.
outcome: RAS design is described as pervasive throughout the POWER4 system, 'as much a part of the design as is anything else'; a companion paper by Bossen et al. covers the full POWER4 RAS feature set.
